title: Optionals
subtitle: Swift's way of making "there might be nothing here" a fact the compiler checks.

sections.body:
An optional is a box that either holds a value or holds nothing. `String` always has a string in it. `String?` might have a string, or might be `nil`.

This sounds small, and it changes everything. In a language without optionals, any object reference might secretly be null, and you find out at runtime when it crashes. In Swift, a type that can be absent *says so in its name*, and the compiler refuses to let you use the value until you've handled the empty case.

So `nil` doesn't disappear. It becomes visible, and the compiler starts helping you.

Think of a PO box.

A `String` is a letter handed to you directly — it's in your hand, it exists.

A `String?` is a PO box. There might be a letter inside, or the box might be empty. You can't read the letter without opening the box first, and you can't assume something's in there just because you were given a key.

Unwrapping is opening the box. Force-unwrapping with `!` is opening it while *promising* there's a letter inside — and if you're wrong, the program stops.

sections.caption: Four ways to open the box — all of them safe.

sections.body:
`Optional` isn't compiler magic. It's an ordinary enum in the standard library:

```
enum Optional<Wrapped> {
    case none
    case some(Wrapped)
}
```

`String?` is sugar for `Optional<String>`, `nil` is sugar for `.none`, and optional binding is sugar for pattern-matching `.some`. That's why you can `switch` over an optional, and why `Optional` gets `map` and `flatMap` like any other container.

The compiler does add one optimisation worth knowing: for class references and other pointer-shaped types, an optional costs *no extra memory*. The all-zeroes pointer is reused to mean `.none`. This is called a spare-bit representation. So `UIView?` is the same size as `UIView` — you're not paying for the safety.

sections.title: Unwrapping an optional
sections.altText: An Optional<String> branches into two cases: .some, holding the string "Ada", which flows to safe use; and .none, which flows to a default value.

steps.caption: An optional is one of exactly two cases.
If a value is present, binding gives you the unwrapped type.
If it's nil, you must say what happens instead — the compiler won't let you skip it.

sections.title: Reaching for ! to make the error go away
sections.body:
`!` doesn't handle the empty case, it asserts the case can't happen. When that assertion is wrong the app crashes with "Unexpectedly found nil" — and it crashes on the user's device, not yours.

`!` is defensible when absence is genuinely a programmer error you want to fail loudly on (an outlet that must be connected, a bundled resource that must exist). It's not a shortcut for "I don't want to write `guard let` right now".

An optional makes absence part of the type, so the compiler forces you to decide what happens when there's nothing there. Every `!` you write is you taking that decision back off the compiler and onto yourself.

title: Closures
subtitle: Functions you can pass around — and the variables they quietly take with them.

sections.body:
A closure is a block of code you can store in a variable, pass to a function, and call later. That much is just "a function without a name".

The important half is in the word *closure*: it closes over the variables around it. When you write a closure that mentions `count`, it doesn't copy the current value of `count` and forget where it came from — it keeps a reference to the actual storage, and keeps that storage alive for as long as the closure exists.

That's what makes closures powerful, and it's also the source of nearly every retain cycle in an iOS codebase.

A closure is a to-do note that says "send the report to Sam".

The note isn't self-contained. It refers to Sam. As long as that note exists in somebody's pocket, Sam has to stick around — you can't dismiss Sam while a note referring to them is still pending.

A capture list is rewriting the note to say "send the report to Sam, but if Sam has already left, just bin the note". Same instruction, but it no longer forces Sam to stay.

sections.caption: `count` outlives `makeCounter` because the returned closure captured it.

sections.heading: Escaping and non-escaping
sections.body:
**Escaping vs non-escaping**

A closure parameter is *non-escaping* by default: the function promises to call it before returning and not store it anywhere. That promise is what lets you use `self` inside without writing `self.`, because there's no way the closure can outlive the call.

Mark it `@escaping` and the promise is gone — the closure may be stored, queued, or called later. Now Swift makes you write `self` explicitly, precisely so that capturing `self` is a visible decision rather than an accident.

That required `self.` isn't bureaucracy. It's the compiler asking: *are you sure you want this object kept alive until this closure runs?*

sections.caption: The compiler forces `self.` in escaping closures so the capture is deliberate.

sections.body:
A closure is two things bolted together: a function pointer, and a heap-allocated *context box* holding the captured variables. Swift calls this pair a thick function value.

That box is reference counted like any object. Captured `var`s are promoted from the stack to that box — which is why `count` in the example survives `makeCounter` returning, and why two closures capturing the same variable genuinely share it rather than each getting a copy.

A non-escaping closure can skip the heap entirely: since it provably doesn't outlive the call, the compiler can keep its context on the stack. That's the real reason non-escaping is the default — it's the faster case, and `@escaping` is you opting into the allocation.

sections.title: Assuming a capture list copies everything
sections.body:
`[weak self]` only changes how `self` is captured. Everything else the closure mentions is still captured strongly, including other objects, and including `self` if you also reference it implicitly through a property.

And `[weak self]` alone doesn't make a closure safe — it makes `self` optional. If the closure fires after `self` is gone, `self?.doThing()` silently does nothing. Sometimes that's exactly right; sometimes it means a callback you were relying on never happened.
A closure captures storage, not values, and keeps that storage alive. Ask of every escaping closure: what does this keep alive, and for how long?

title: Struct vs Class
subtitle: Value semantics versus reference semantics, and why Swift pushes you toward structs.

sections.body:
A struct is a *value*. When you assign it or pass it to a function, you get an independent copy. Changing the copy can't affect the original.

A class is a *reference*. When you assign it, both names point at the same object in memory. Changing it through one name changes it for everyone holding a reference.

Everything else — inheritance, deinit, reference counting, identity — follows from that one difference. Swift makes structs the default because most of the time, shared mutable state is a liability you didn't ask for.

A struct is a printed document. Hand someone a copy and scribble on yours — theirs is untouched. There's no such thing as "the" document; there are just documents that happen to have the same contents.

A class is a shared Google Doc. Send someone the link and you're both looking at the same thing. When they edit a paragraph it changes under you, whether or not you were looking. That's useful when you *want* one shared truth, and dangerous when you don't.

sections.caption: The `let` difference surprises people more than the copy does.

sections.title: Copy versus share
sections.altText: Two struct variables a and b each point at their own separate storage. Two class variables c and d both point at one shared object.

steps.caption: Assigning a struct copies the storage — two variables, two boxes.
Assigning a class copies the pointer — two variables, one box.

sections.body:
Structs don't automatically live on the stack, and classes aren't automatically slow. The real distinctions are:

**Allocation.** A class instance is always a heap allocation with a reference count and a type header. A struct is stored inline wherever it lives — on the stack as a local, or inside its owner's memory as a property. A struct property inside a class instance is on the heap too.

**Copy on write.** Standard-library collections are structs, but copying an `Array` doesn't copy its elements. Both copies share one buffer, and the buffer is only duplicated when one of them is mutated *and* the reference count says it isn't uniquely held. That's why value semantics stay affordable at scale — and you can implement the same trick yourself with `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`.

**Dispatch.** A method on a `final class` or a struct can be called directly. A non-final class method goes through a vtable so subclasses can override it.

sections.title: Reaching for a class because "the data is big"
sections.body:
Copy-on-write means a struct holding an array or string isn't copied wholesale on assignment — only the small outer value is, and the shared buffer is duplicated lazily on mutation.

Pick a class when you need *identity* (this is the same object, not merely an equal one), shared mutable state that many owners must observe, a deinit, or Objective-C interop. Size alone is rarely the reason.

Default to a struct. Reach for a class when you specifically need identity, shared mutation, inheritance, or deinit — and know that you're taking on reference counting and the possibility of cycles when you do.

title: Protocols
subtitle: Describing what a type can do, so code can depend on behaviour instead of concrete types.

sections.body:
A protocol is a list of requirements — methods, properties, initialisers — that a conforming type promises to provide. Code written against the protocol works with any type that conforms, present or future.

In an object-oriented language you'd reach for a base class here. Protocols do the job without the inheritance: a struct can conform, an enum can conform, a type can conform to many protocols, and you can add conformance to a type you don't own via an extension. That's why Swift can push value types so hard and still let you abstract.

The everyday payoff is testability. A view model that depends on `ContentLoading` rather than `NetworkContentLoader` can be handed a stub in a test without a server in sight.

A protocol is a job description, not a job title.

"Must be able to take payment and issue a receipt" describes what you need. A card reader satisfies it, a cash till satisfies it, and so does a person with a notebook. You wrote the shop's process against the description, so you can swap the implementation without rewriting the process.

Inheritance, by contrast, is "must be a kind of till" — which rules out the notebook even though it would have worked fine.

sections.caption: Conformance is opt-in and additive — including for types you didn't write.

sections.heading: some versus any
sections.body:
**`some` versus `any`**

`some ContentLoading` means *one specific conforming type, chosen at compile time*. The compiler knows exactly which type it is, so the call is static and there's no box. This is an opaque type, and it's shorthand for a generic parameter.

`any ContentLoading` means *any conforming type, possibly different each time*. The value is wrapped in an existential box and calls go through a witness table at runtime. That flexibility costs an indirection — and it's what you need when you're storing a heterogeneous array of conformers.

Rule of thumb: `some` when there's one type and the caller doesn't need to know it, `any` when the type genuinely varies at runtime.

sections.caption: `some` and generics are the same mechanism seen from two directions.

sections.body:
Calling a method through `any Protocol` uses a *witness table*: a table of function pointers, one per requirement, produced when the type declares conformance. The existential value carries a pointer to the value (or the value inline if it's small enough for the three-word buffer) plus a pointer to that table.

With `some Protocol` or a generic parameter, the compiler knows the concrete type at the call site, so it can look the witness up statically and often inline it entirely.

A protocol with associated types or `Self` requirements couldn't be used as `any` at all before Swift 5.7, because the box has no way to express "and the element type is the same one you got last time". It's allowed now, but the compiler asks you to open the existential before using those members — which is why you sometimes need a generic function to do the work.

sections.title: Writing a protocol for one implementation
sections.body:
A protocol with exactly one conformer and no test double isn't abstraction, it's an extra file to keep in sync. Every call now has an indirection you can't follow in the editor without a jump.

Add the protocol when there's a second implementation — including a test stub, which counts. Until then the concrete type is easier to read and trivially easy to extract later.

Protocols let code depend on behaviour rather than concrete types, without inheritance. Use `some` when one type is involved and `any` only when the type genuinely varies at runtime — and don't add a protocol until there's a second implementation.
